messages.subject: bug with num.threads>1 on a Mac
messages.subject_clean: bug with num.threads>1 on a Mac
messages.body_plain:
Hi R-inla group,

I seem to have found a bug that occurs on my 8-core Mac when I use more than 1 thread, but it doesn't occur on my coworker's 4-core Linux computer. I see in the documentation that num.threads defaults to 1 in Windows; maybe it should on a Mac too? I get inconsistent and inaccurate fixed effect estimates when I use the default or if I specify num.threads=6. I get consistent and decent estimates if I only use 1 core. I didn't try it with intermediate numbers of cores. If I reduce the number of observations and random effect levels, the bug goes away. This is the example.

library(INLA)

simfun0 <- function(beta=c(2,1),

                   sd.re <http://sd.re>=5,

                   ngrp=10,nobs=200,

                   invlink=exp) {

    x <- rnorm(nobs)

    f <- factor(rep(1:ngrp,nobs/ngrp))

    u <- rnorm(ngrp,sd=sd.re <http://sd.re>)

    eta <- beta[1]+beta[2]*x+u[f]

    mu <- invlink(eta)

    return(data.frame(x,f,mu))

}

#ngrp <- 1000; nobs <- 2000; phi <- 0.1

ngrp <- 1000; nobs <- 20000; phi <- 0.1

set.seed(101)

dd0 <- simfun0(nobs=nobs, ngrp=ngrp)

dd <- data.frame(dd0,y=rnbinom(nobs,size=phi,mu=dd0$mu))

set.seed(101)

inlam1 <- inla(y~x+f(f,model="iid"),family=list(family="nbinomial"),

                   data=dd, num.threads=1)

summary(inlam1)

set.seed(101)

inlam2 <- inla(y~x+f(f,model="iid"),family=list(family="nbinomial"),

                   data=dd, num.threads=1)

summary(inlam2)

set.seed(101)

inlam3 <- inla(y~x+f(f,model="iid"),family=list(family="nbinomial"),

                   data=dd, num.threads=6)

summary(inlam3)

set.seed(101)

inlam4 <- inla(y~x+f(f,model="iid"),family=list(family="nbinomial"),

                   data=dd, num.threads=6)

summary(inlam4)

messages.subject: Interactions and linear combinations in a joint likelihood model
messages.subject_clean: Interactions and linear combinations in a joint likelihood model
messages.body_plain:
Greetings all,

I have a question about the proper procedure for examining interactions within the context of a joint likelihood model. The following is example code for a model where the first stage is a 0/1 binary dependent variable, and then the second stage with a continuous dependent variable only for observations where u_i == 1 at the first stage. The basic procedure borrows from the code found in the Blangiardi/Cameletti book. In any case, I wish to generate and then plot marginal effects for an interaction term that is present in both stages of the model. The way that I can get the models with linear combinations (rr and rr2) to run without an error message is to index the linear combinations row-wise by stage (i.e., 1:n, or (n+1:n*2)).

So, I have two (probably rudimentary) questions:

1. Is this procedure correct, or is something different required for the joint likelihood model?

n = 100
u <- (rnorm(n)>0) + 0
y <- rgamma(n,10)
y[u==0] <- NA
idat <- list(Y=matrix(NA,2*n,2))
idat$Y[1:n,1] <- u
idat$Y[n+1:n,2] <- y
idat$mu.u <- rep(1:0, each=n)
idat$mu.y <- rep(0:1, each=n)

idat$u_violation <- c((rnorm(n)>0) + 0, rep(0,n))
idat$y_violation <- c(rep(0,n),idat$u_violation[1:n])

idat$u_revenue <- c(runif(n,0,100), rep(0,n))
idat$y_revenue <- c(rep(0,n),idat$u_revenue[1:n])
form = Y ~ 0 + mu.u + mu.y + u_revenue + y_revenue + u_violation + y_violation +
  u_revenue:u_violation + y_revenue:y_violation

r = inla(form,c('binomial', 'gamma'),
           data=idat,control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),verbose=F)
lc_u = inla.make.lincombs(
  u_revenue =  r$model.matrix[1:n, "u_revenue"],
  `u_revenue:u_violation` =  r$model.matrix[1:n, "u_revenue:u_violation"])

lc_y = inla.make.lincombs(
  y_revenue =  r$model.matrix[(n+1):(n*2), "y_revenue"],
  `y_revenue:y_violation` =  r$model.matrix[(n+1):(n*2), "y_revenue:y_violation"])

rr = inla(form,c('binomial', 'gamma'),
    data=idat,control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),verbose=F,lincomb = lc_u)

rr2 = inla(form,c('binomial', 'gamma'),
          data=idat,control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),verbose=F,lincomb = lc_y)

2. Am I correct in assuming then that the following code then plots the posterior density of the revenue parameter for the first stage of the model, for non-violators and then for violators?

plot(density(rr$summary.lincomb.derived$mean[idat$u_violation[1:100]==0]),ylim=c(0,2))
lines(density(rr$summary.lincomb.derived$mean[idat$u_violation[1:100]==1]),col='red')

thank you for your time.

messages.subject: Multilevel spatial model
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am running a spatial (CAR) model on a data structure that has two conceptual levels: counties (cid) nested within states (sid). I want to include a spatial random effect at the county-level and a non-spatial random effect at the state-level. Here is what my formula looks like:

form <- out ~ 1 + f(cid, model = "bym", graph = "nb.adj") + f(sid, model = "iid")

Does this make sense?

Thanks.

Best,
Shige

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] bug with num.threads>1 on a Mac
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] bug with num.threads>1 on a Mac
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

in the INLA algorithm there is an optimization within an optimization.
and the initial value for the inner optimisation is previous optimum.
the issue is when running this in parallel then esentiallt the initial
value is kind of random due to the thread id. this can lead to minor
differences, but in your case more large ones. the way out is to set to
inner optimisation tolerance to something insane small, like

	control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-12)

then it will stop when it cannot improve the inner optimstion any more.

let me know if this does not fix your problem.  I would also recommend
to update to the most recent testing version.

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Finn & others,

 Xavier and I have been working on this binomial-binomial model with two misaligned point patterns. The predictions don't quite fit what I'd expect. When I run a 'simple' model, just a single binomial model with only stk.y, my predictions fall within a 0.02 to 0.04 range for fitted values, which corresponds pretty closely to the range of risk in the study population. When I do this double model, however, I get a very narrow prediction that falls in a different range than what I'd expect:

> range(m.prd)

[1] 0.499999999730990 0.499999999778862

> range(sd.prd)

[1] 0.000728774754394849 0.000886545272648484

Model hyperparameters:

                        mean        sd 0.025quant  0.5quant 0.975quant      mode

Range for xi.field 1.470e+04 7.679e+03  5305.4759 1.291e+04  3.438e+04 1.012e+04

Stdev for xi.field 4.291e-01 1.259e-01     0.2389 4.098e-01  7.284e-01 3.736e-01

Range for x.field  7.631e+03 1.107e+04   986.0969 4.392e+03  3.415e+04 2.093e+03

Stdev for x.field  1.754e-01 1.144e-01     0.0353 1.500e-01  4.648e-01 9.520e-02

Beta for u.field   1.252e+00 2.055e-01     0.8428 1.254e+00  1.650e+00 1.262e+00

Compute corrected stdev for theta[0]: negative 1.202842  positive 0.869014

Compute corrected stdev for theta[1]: negative 0.984359  positive 1.042373

Compute corrected stdev for theta[2]: negative 1.307514  positive 0.679840

Compute corrected stdev for theta[3]: negative 0.760624  positive 0.935674

Compute corrected stdev for theta[4]: negative 0.813922  positive 1.086136

The current version of the script is below:

stk.y <- inla.stack(tag='est.y',
                    data=list(y=cbind(data$result, NA), link=1),
                    A=list(A.y, 1),
                    effects=list(xi.field=1:spde2$n.spde,
                                list(intercept.y = rep(1, 19532))))

stk.x <- inla.stack(data=list(y=cbind(NA, cmv$result), link=2),
                    A = list(A.x, 1),
                    tag ='est.x',
                    effects=list(list(u.field=1:spde2$n.spde,
                                      x.field=1:spde2$n.spde),
                                 list(intercept.x = rep(1, 2223))))
grid$na1<-NA
grid$na2<-NA
NAgrid<-as.matrix(cbind(grid$na1, grid$na2))
stk.p <- inla.stack(tag='prediction',
                         data=list(y=NAgrid, link=1),
                         A=list(A.pred, 1),
                         effects=list(list(xi.field=1:spde2$n.spde),
                         list(intercept = rep(1, length(grid$id)))))

stk <- inla.stack.join(stk.x, stk.y, stk.p)

form_mis <- y ~ -1 +  intercept.x +intercept.y +
  f(xi.field, model=spde2) +
  f(x.field, model=spde2) +
  f(u.field, copy='xi.field', fixed=FALSE)

model_mis <- inla(form_mis, data=inla.stack.data(stk), family=rep('binomial',2),
                  control.predictor=list(compute=FALSE, A=inla.stack.A(stk),
                                         link=inla.stack.data(stk)$link),
                  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic=TRUE, config=TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
                  verbose = FALSE)

messages.subject: spatial field varies across years
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I built a model assuming that the spatial field is constant over year:
form.1 <-  y ~ 0 + b0 +  f(year, model="iid") + f(s, model=spde)

The effect of year and spatial field are shown in the following plots:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-BlvSoj88HdM/WOZhMCHEfCI/AAAAAAAAAcQ/kzjbZns9R80tKs_jIWMpfrLHKxlFuafXQCLcB/s1600/5.year.jpeg>

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-C1F2H2vOA4Q/WOZhTNnjS4I/AAAAAAAAAcU/n-l26nsydmAz1ZZgngjiw27mq9G3wP7GwCLcB/s1600/5.ymean.jpeg>

In comparison, I built another model to allow the spatial field to vary across years:
form.2 <-  y ~ 0 + b0 +  f(year, model="iid") + f(s, model=spde, replicate=s.repl)

The effect of year and spatial field are

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-wZH-p-Ro4C0/WOZiFFxJGxI/AAAAAAAAAcc/PlTqETvfzk8c9qO8NTGVdm0mazUIsVpbgCLcB/s1600/4.year.jpeg>

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-MWYGGhhtPdg/WOZihRM0ldI/AAAAAAAAAcg/OpQ321WqDiQH6gQL0WoJvyHpJ8y0v3UpgCLcB/s1600/Screenshot%2B2017-04-06%2B11.44.37.png>It seems like that in the second model, the year effect was included in the spatial field, so the year effect was nearly zero and the spatial effect was negative. <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-MWYGGhhtPdg/WOZihRM0ldI/AAAAAAAAAcg/OpQ321WqDiQH6gQL0WoJvyHpJ8y0v3UpgCLcB/s1600/Screenshot%2B2017-04-06%2B11.44.37.png>Is there any way to allow me to maintain the year effect in the first plot and still get changing spatial field across years? <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-MWYGGhhtPdg/WOZihRM0ldI/AAAAAAAAAcg/OpQ321WqDiQH6gQL0WoJvyHpJ8y0v3UpgCLcB/s1600/Screenshot%2B2017-04-06%2B11.44.37.png>

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial field varies across years
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
yes, your spatio-temporal model is confounded with the year effect. You can impose
a simple integrate-to-zero constraint on the spatial fields, via
  spde <- inla.spde2.(pc)matern(..., constr=TRUE)

Also note that if you have an intercept in the model (b0 in your formula I presume) then
your year effect will _also_ be confounded with the intercept; rw2 models have a default sum-to-zero constraint, but not iid models.
In my attached test case, I left out b0 instead of imposing additional constraints on the year effect.

Empirical, unconstrained, and spde-constrained estimates below. See attached file for full example.

Finn

        1         2
 53.93857 354.92855

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 2017-04-04 at 10:47 -0700, Tyler Scott wrote:
> Greetings all,
>
> I have a question about the proper procedure for examining
> interactions within the context of a joint likelihood model. The
> following is example code for a model where the first stage is a 0/1
> binary dependent variable, and then the second stage with a
> continuous dependent variable only for observations where u_i == 1 at
> the first stage. The basic procedure borrows from the code found in
> the Blangiardi/Cameletti book. In any case, I wish to generate and
> then plot marginal effects for an interaction term that is present in
> both stages of the model. The way that I can get the models with
> linear combinations (rr and rr2) to run without an error message is
> to index the linear combinations row-wise by stage (i.e., 1:n, or
> (n+1:n*2)).
>
> So, I have two (probably rudimentary) questions:
>
> 1. Is this procedure correct, or is something different required for
> the joint likelihood model?
>
> n = 100
> u <- (rnorm(n)>0) + 0
> y <- rgamma(n,10)
> y[u==0] <- NA
> idat <- list(Y=matrix(NA,2*n,2))
> idat$Y[1:n,1] <- u
> idat$Y[n+1:n,2] <- y
> idat$mu.u <- rep(1:0, each=n)
> idat$mu.y <- rep(0:1, each=n)
>
> idat$u_violation <- c((rnorm(n)>0) + 0, rep(0,n))
> idat$y_violation <- c(rep(0,n),idat$u_violation[1:n])
>
> idat$u_revenue <- c(runif(n,0,100), rep(0,n))
> idat$y_revenue <- c(rep(0,n),idat$u_revenue[1:n])
> form = Y ~ 0 + mu.u + mu.y + u_revenue + y_revenue + u_violation +
> y_violation +
>   u_revenue:u_violation + y_revenue:y_violation
>
> r = inla(form,c('binomial', 'gamma'),
>            data=idat,control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),verbose=F)
> lc_u = inla.make.lincombs(
>   u_revenue =  r$model.matrix[1:n, "u_revenue"],
>   `u_revenue:u_violation` =  r$model.matrix[1:n,
> "u_revenue:u_violation"])
>
> lc_y = inla.make.lincombs(
>   y_revenue =  r$model.matrix[(n+1):(n*2), "y_revenue"],
>   `y_revenue:y_violation` =  r$model.matrix[(n+1):(n*2),
> "y_revenue:y_violation"])
>
> rr = inla(form,c('binomial', 'gamma'),
>     data=idat,control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),verbose=F,lincomb
> = lc_u)
>
> rr2 = inla(form,c('binomial', 'gamma'),
>
> data=idat,control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),verbose=F,lincomb =
> lc_y)

Hi

this seems correct. You can, if you want, merge, lc_y and lc_u, if you
give them different names, so you only need one call to inla() again,
like

> names(lc_u) = paste('u', 1:length(lc_u), sep="")
> names(lc_y) = paste('y', 1:length(lc_y), sep="")
> lc = c(lc_u, lc_y)

but if you're unsure about the valididity of the results, just compute
the mean using the mean of fixed effects, and, artificially just make
sure the interaction is orthogonal or almost so, to the fixed effects
(just for testing) and then the variance is just the sum.

> 2. Am I correct in assuming then that the following code then plots
> the posterior density of the revenue parameter for the first stage of
> the model, for non-violators and then for violators?
>
> plot(density(rr$summary.lincomb.derived$mean[idat$u_violation[1:100]=
> =0]),ylim=c(0,2))
> lines(density(rr$summary.lincomb.derived$mean[idat$u_violation[1:100]
> ==1]),col='red')

this I am unsure about, since

> sum(idat$u_violation[1:100]==0)
[1] 53

but the plot, will only plot one marginal. may you want a loop ???

best
H

messages.subject: Spatial field confounded with predictor variables
messages.subject_clean: Spatial field confounded with predictor variables
messages.body_plain:
Greetings and thank you in advance for advice.

I am asking the research question "Are there less birds along portions of the coast that are more degraded?"

My data is a long-term set of observations describing bird counts at ~25 sections of coastline along 1000 miles of a coast the runs primarily north to south. Observations were often repeated at the same sections of coastline (exact locations varied slightly within these coastal sections) over many years. Simple data exploration suggests that there are less birds along sections of the coast that are more degraded.

The variables are:
Response: Bird presence (and bird counts when present)
Spatial index: Latitude
Temporal index: Year
Covariates: Day of year (abundances peak in spring/summer); DegraderPC1 (higher = more degraded); DegraderPC2 (higher = more degraded).

The data is zero inflated and am fitting a binomial model on presence/absence data and a negative binomial model when birds are present (i.e., a hurdle model). For brevity, I will discuss here only the binomial model component, which is essentially parameterized the same as the negative binomial model.

DegraderPC1 and DegraderPC2 are orthogonal principal components describing types of habitat degradation. Even though the data has been collected for 25 years, we have only one measure of DegraderPC1 and DegraderPC2 for each section of coast, and thus for every observation at that section of coast assume the same DegraderPC1 and DegraderPC2 values (i.e., we assume that that coastal section has maintained the same level of degradation for the entire time series).

My approach was to:
(1) fit a one dimensional mesh to the data based on the latitude of the observations, (one dimension rather than two since I am describing an essentially linear range of habitat (a coast the runs north to south)),
(2) allow the spatial field to vary year-to-year according to an AR1 process,
(3) treat day of year as a RW2 process to allow abundances to peak in the spring/summer,
and (4) estimate parameters for my main (fixed) effects of interest: DegraderPC1 and DegraderPC2, which I anticipate to be negative.

The basic code is thus:

meshBird<-inla.mesh.1d(as.matrix(Bird$Latitude))
spdeBird<-inla.spde2.matern(meshBird)
A.Bird<-
  inla.spde.make.A(meshBird,
                   loc=as.matrix(Bird$Latitude),
                   group=Bird$Year,
                   n.group = 25) #25 years in the dataset
field.indiciesBird<-inla.spde.make.index("field",n.spde=meshBird$n,n.group=25)
stack.Bird=
  inla.stack(
    data=list(Presence.Absence=Bird$Presence.Absence),
    A=list(A.Bird,1),
    effects=list(c(field.indiciesBird,
                   list(Intercept=1)),
                 list(data.frame(
                   DegraderPC1=Bird$DegraderPC1,
                   DegraderPC2=Bird$DegraderPC2,
                   day.of.year=Bird$day.of.year,
                   Year=Bird$Year))))
formulaBird<-Presence.Absence ~ -1 + Intercept  + DegraderPC1 + DegraderPC2 +
  f(field,model=spdeBird,group=field.group,control.group=list(model="ar1"))+
  f(day.of.year,model="rw2"))
modBird<-inla(formulaBird,
                 data=inla.stack.data(stack.Bird,spde=Bird),
                 family="binomial",
                 control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.Bird),
                                          compute=TRUE))
summary(modBird)

The problem is that I am getting positive parameter estimates for the DegraderPCs (i.e., the model says that there are more birds along coasts that are more degraded), which is the opposite of what simple data exploration shows and is counterintuitive. When I examine estimates for the spatial field (i.e., how does bird presence vary by latitude?) it shows a pattern that is virtually the opposite of how DegraderPC1 varies with latitude. In other words, the model appears to be attributing low presence of birds at degraded sections of coast due to a spatial effect rather than because that section of coast is more degraded, and then as an artifact estimates birds to be more likely to be present at more degraded sections of coast. Unfortunately, there is a pattern that portions of the coast at the northern and southern ends of my spatial range are more degraded, so I'm not sure whether increasing the smoothing of the spatial field will resolve this.

My question is, is there any way to resolve this while addressing the spatiotemporal structure in my dataset? That is, I want my analysis to account for the premise that observations at proximate sections of coast (and years) will be similar. The alternative seems to be to ignore the spatial component and refit the model treating the sections of coast as iid models, and acknowledge the caveat of spatial non-independence this in the paper.

Again, thank you very much for the help.

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial field confounded with predictor variables
messages.body_plain:
To deal with such spatial confounding, I suggest two things:
1) be more careful with the priors. Currently you're not explicitly specifying the field parameter priors at all. I also suggest looking at inla.spde2.pcmatern for a better prior distribution model.
2) impose integration constraints on the field model. constr=TRUE in
inla.spde2.(pc)matern imposes an integrate-to-zero constraint, but you can also
impose orthogonal-to-covariates constraints via either extraconstr or extraconstr.int <http://extraconstr.int> where the latter gives integral constrains, like
\int field(s) covariate(s) ds = 0

Finn

messages.subject: combining predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am creating counterfactual scenarios combining different predictions in a dataset: number of deaths by age that then I use to compute life expectancies.

I know that I can summarize individual predictions, but I wonder if there is a way to get values from the distribution of predicted values in order to combine them later (e.g., life expectancy) and get the uncertainty of that combination or compute other quantities of interest (e.g., difference in life expectancy between groups or different values of covariates and its uncertainty).

I am doing this, but I don't know if it is correct:

> set.seed(10304)

> # complete data
> n = 10
> x = rnorm(n)
> y = 1 + x + rnorm(n)
> r = inla(y ~ 1 + x, data = data.frame(x,y))
>
> # add scenarios to predict
> xx = c(x, 10, 20)
> yy = c(y, NA, NA)
> rr = inla(yy ~ 1 + xx, data = data.frame(xx,yy),
+           control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
+           control.compute = list(config=TRUE))
>
> # predicted values
> rr$summary.linear.predictor[n+1,]
                 mean       sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant     mode          kld
Predictor.11 15.04227 6.298533   2.470227 15.04013   27.63636 15.03885 9.826833e-07
> rr$summary.linear.predictor[n+2,]
                 mean       sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant     mode          kld
Predictor.12 28.95189 12.37504   4.250969  28.9477   53.69612 28.94519 9.826603e-07

> # get posterior sample
> x = inla.posterior.sample(1000, rr)

> # extract values
> xx1 = NULL
> xx2 = NULL
> for (i in 1:1000) {
+  xx1 <- c(xx1, x[[i]]$latent[11])
+  xx2 <- c(xx2, x[[i]]$latent[12])
+ }
>
> quantile(xx1, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
     2.5%       50%     97.5%
 3.424852 15.035229 27.204548
> quantile(xx2, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
     2.5%       50%     97.5%
 6.259592 28.934255 52.524622
> quantile(xx2-xx1, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
    2.5%      50%    97.5%
 2.63805 13.87995 25.91359

The median and upper bound look right. The lower bound always look off. I don't know why.

Thanks!
Sebastian

Dear all

My crash problems seem to resolve.

I tried a larger Linux computer. That did not help (which means Bill Gates is not to blame, my Win7 PC is ok).

>From other modeling experience I know that numerical problems easily arise when models are poor. I guess this is the main crash reason. It is sligthly annoying that INLA does not tell in more detail what goes wrong, when it crashes. That might leave a clue of better model specification. But anyway it is the modeler's responsibility to specify the decent model. INLA will not give me the correct model, only the parameters of the model that I specify.

In my case it seems promising to combine site-specific random errors with a relatively sparse mesh for a spatio-temporal random field.

best
Øyvind

On Mon, 2017-04-10 at 01:39 -0700, Øyvind wrote:
> Dear all
>
> My crash problems seem to resolve.
>
> I tried a larger Linux computer. That did not help (which means Bill
> Gates is not to blame, my Win7 PC is ok).
>
> From other modeling experience I know that numerical problems easily
> arise when models are poor. I guess this is the main crash reason. It
> is sligthly annoying that INLA does not tell in more detail what goes
> wrong, when it crashes. That might leave a clue of better model
> specification. But anyway it is the modeler's responsibility to
> specify the decent model. INLA will not give me the correct model,
> only the parameters of the model that I specify.
>

so what does the output with verbose=T  says?

--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

> > >
> > > # Data
> > > yp <- read.csv("yp.csv")

> > > z <- (yp$catch>0) +0
> > > y <- ifelse(yp$catch>0,yp$catch,NA)
> > >
> > > # create mesh
> > > points = as.matrix(yp[,c("X","Y")])
> > > bnd = inla.nonconvex.hull(points,convex=0.2)

> > >
> > > # define SPDE
> > > spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh, constr=TRUE)
> > >
> > > # Observation matrix $A$ for each year
> > > table(repl <- yp$year-(min(yp$year)-1))
> > > A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, repl=repl, loc=as.matrix(yp[,c("X","Y")]))
> > >
> > > # Spatial index
> > > indz <- inla.spde.make.index(name='sz', n.spde=spde$n.spde, n.repl=n.year)
> > > indy <- inla.spde.make.index(name='sy', n.spde=spde$n.spde, n.repl=n.year)
> > >
> > > # Stack data
> > > stk.z <- inla.stack(tag='est.z',
> > >                       data=list(z=z, y=cbind(z,NA),link=1),
> > >                       A=list(A,1),
> > >                       effects=list(indz,
> > >                                    list(z.b0=rep(1,length(z)),
> > >                                         depth.z=yp$depth,
> > >                                         secchi.z=yp$secchi,
> > >                                         geartemp.z=yp$geartemp,
> > >                                         do_gear.z=yp$do_gear,
> > >                                         geardepth.z=yp$geardepth,
> > >                                         year.z=yp$year)))
> > > stk.y <- inla.stack(tag='est.y',
> > >                       data=list(c=y, y=cbind(NA,y), link=2),
> > >                       A=list(A,1),
> > >                       effects=list(indy,
> > >                                    list(y.b0=rep(1,length(y)),
> > >                                         depth.y=yp$depth,
> > >                                         secchi.y=yp$secchi,
> > >                                         geartemp.y=yp$geartemp,
> > >                                         do_gear.y=yp$do_gear,
> > >                                         geardepth.y=yp$geardepth,
> > >                                         year.y=yp$year.num)))
> > > stk.zy <- inla.stack(stk.z,stk.y)
> > >
> > > ## Jointly model
> > > form <-  y ~ -1 + depth.z + secchi.z + geartemp.z + do_gear.z + geardepth.z + f(year.z, model="iid") + depth.y + secchi.y + geartemp.y + do_gear.y + geardepth.y + f(year.y, model="iid") + f(sy, model=spde, replicate=sy.repl) + f(sz, copy='sy', replicate=sz.repl,fixed=FALSE)

> > > Ruby

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial field varies across years
messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

I just changed the model form by changing "iid" to "rw2" and adding the intercept.

form <-  y ~ 0 + z.b0 + depth.z + secchi.z + geartemp.z + do_gear.z + geardepth.z + f(year.z, model="rw2") + y.b0 + depth.y + secchi.y + geartemp.y + do_gear.y + geardepth.y + f(year.y, model="rw2") + f(sy, model=spde, replicate=sy.repl) + f(sz, copy='sy', replicate=sz.repl,fixed=FALSE)

The year effects of the joint model:
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-JLAq3Ia7YSE/WOun1FM25cI/AAAAAAAAAeU/C5278ksqH000Bu0LimKQno3s5kKBL4XIgCLcB/s1600/yz_year.png>
The spatial field of z:
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Yvhzs-4A3Sw/WOuoC-BRksI/AAAAAAAAAec/1qP-XyVux8wq3QxBOONCWii10QBBHssxACLcB/s1600/z_joint.png>

The spatial field of y:
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-g2BdDDe5JS8/WOuoRfqpKjI/AAAAAAAAAeg/YcRaNDlqraUVcYQedz2JSytNPx7uzK9iQCLcB/s1600/y_joint.png>

I also run models only with z or y.

The year effect of z-only model:
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-6QZWAmRF39w/WOuohRzuXDI/AAAAAAAAAek/qVOl5XpMAKUG7p6-2KCHa35M75Jm_lUvwCLcB/s1600/z_year_rw2.png>

Spatial field of z:
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-ZoU1nL_6MlE/WOuottaQg-I/AAAAAAAAAeo/LQJBTJiUe3UepZ5x37tBZMfYsV4kjnocQCLcB/s1600/z_only.png>
The year effect of y-only model:
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-mryb9Jra7lA/WOuo8zWXTwI/AAAAAAAAAes/-S_SDgAlaXY2iijGbfuactYqne3ra9BuQCLcB/s1600/y_year_rw2.png>

Spatial field of y:
 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-QWJpihq0lw4/WOupS-LVBFI/AAAAAAAAAe0/d4t6Fk7sSgAZXs2cldW45tYFSuw1fvWAACLcB/s1600/y_only.png>
The results seem good for me. But I am not sure if there are any hidden problems...

form <-  y ~ 0 + z.b0 + depth.z + secchi.z + geartemp.z + do_gear.z + geardepth.z + f(year.z, model="rw2")

messages.subject: Barrier models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to try some barrier models on some dataset I have. Where could I find some R code with some examples? The section in the R website seems to be under construction at the moment.

Also, how scalable are these models? I am planning to use them on some noise data from my hometown where we have ~4000 buildings according to Open Street Map...

Many thanks.

Virgilio

messages.body_plain:
Hi Virgilio,

Yes, the website is actually under replacement :)

See https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic107.html
- here you find a code example (comparing the different models) and links to explanations for the mesh
- the dataset/analysis is further explained in https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03787

Let me know if you have any questions or feedback to the new site.

# Scalability

This should work on the same kind of problems as the stationary model. It will be slower, perhaps something like 3x.

Kind regards,
Haakon

messages.subject: Units for matern2d latent model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am fitting a spatial model to a grid using the matern2d model.
Am I correct in assuming that the units for the range are numbers of grid cells? e.g. If I have grid cells that are 600*600 metres, and the mode of the posterior estimate for the range is 10, then that represents a range of 6000 metres?

Here is the full model call:

y <- inla.matrix2vector(ymat)
x <- inla.matrix2vector(xmat)
node <- which(!is.na <http://is.na>(y))
dat <- data.frame(x = x, y = y, node = node)

form <- y ~ x + offset(xoffset) +
    f(node, model = "matern2d", nu = 1, nrow = nrow, ncol = ncol,
        hyper = list(range = list(param = c(1,1),
        prior = "loggamma",
        initial = 1),
        prec = list(param = c(1,1))))

m1 <- inla(form, family = 'poisson', data = dat,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1), keep = F)

#Plot posterior density for range:
plot(m1$marginals.hyperpar[[2]], type = 'l')

where ymat is the spatial grid (as a matrix) for the response values, xmat is grid for a predictor and node is a vector of positions for where we have observations.

Thanks,
Chris

about constraints for replicate models; the constraints are also
replicated. the same is the case with group.

from what I read out of the discussion, the results seems ok in the
sense that if the spatial field is replicated over years, then the
'year effect' would be smoohter, since some of the variation over year
is going into the non-zero mean of the spatial effect. if you use
constr=TRUE, ie constraining each realisation of the spatial model to
sum to zero, then I'll guess you'll get something inbetween these two
results.

Best
Håvard

Hi

the unit is 1, so a range 10 are 10 units or grid cells.

I would rather use the spde-models instead... which do the same but
more efficiently and more general

H

On Tue, 2017-04-11 at 18:09 -0700, Chris Brown wrote:
> Hello,
> I am fitting a spatial model to a grid using the matern2d model.
> Am I correct in assuming that the units for the range are numbers of
> grid cells? e.g. If I have grid cells that are 600*600 metres, and
> the mode of the posterior estimate for the range is 10, then that
> represents a range of 6000 metres?
>
> Here is the full model call:
>
> y <- inla.matrix2vector(ymat)
> x <- inla.matrix2vector(xmat)
> node <- which(!is.na <http://is.na>(y))
> dat <- data.frame(x = x, y = y, node = node)
>
> form <- y ~ x + offset(xoffset) +
>     f(node, model = "matern2d", nu = 1, nrow = nrow, ncol = ncol,
>         hyper = list(range = list(param = c(1,1),
>         prior = "loggamma",
>         initial = 1),
>         prec = list(param = c(1,1))))
>
> m1 <- inla(form, family = 'poisson', data = dat,
>     control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1), keep = F)
>
> #Plot posterior density for range:
> plot(m1$marginals.hyperpar[[2]], type = 'l')
>
> where ymat is the spatial grid (as a matrix) for the response values,
> xmat is grid for a predictor and node is a vector of positions for
> where we have observations.

messages.subject: call INLA in a cluster
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to run my model in a Linux cluster. However, when I run the R script:
library(INLA)
mesh <- inla.mesh.create(globe=1)

It shows an error message:

/home/Rlibs/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/fmesher: /lib64/libstdc++.so.6: version `GLIBCXX_3.4.21' not found (required by /home/Rlibs/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/fmesher)

Error in fmesher.read(prefix, "manifold") :

  File '/tmp/Rtmp0udMce/fmesher10e786323da71.manifold' does not exist.

Calls: inla.mesh.create -> system.time -> fmesher.read

Does anyone have the same experience?

Ruby

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] call INLA in a cluster
messages.body_plain:
This is a _very_ common general error message, so google tells us that
the libstdc++ version you have is old, which is quite common on rarely
updated clusters. Check for example
  strings /lib64/libstdc++.so.6 | grep GLIBCXX

I believe some of these situations can be worked around by calling
  INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround()
to configure INLA to use statically linked binaries.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
If you upgrade INLA to the most recent testing version, hopefully this
would work.

otherwise, you can use the static builds, like

> library(INLA)
> INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround()

and then proceed.

the reason is that you linux distribution is pretty old...

H

messages.subject: Species distribution modeling in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hello

I am building a habitat suitability model (species distribution model) for a particular mosquito species.

Below is a brief description of my data.
data on the presence of the mosquito species in a particular location is collected from different sources.
pseudo absence points are also generated.
using known climatic conditions known to influence the habitat of the species, i want to build a presence absence (0/1) suitability model in INLA.

I have been able to do that using different machine learning algorithms, wondered if its possible to build such kind of a model in INLA. If its possible, how would i specify my model.

Thank you.

Thomas.

messages.subject: Re: Species distribution modeling in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

You can do SDMs perfectly well through INLA (I have done it already several times.)
As far as I know, regarding specifically Bayesian geostatistical models, the first published paper applying this kind of idea through INLA was those of Muñoz et al. (see paper Paper 1 <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00477-012-0652-3>). After that, it has been increasingly used in fisheries science. Mrs. Maria G. Pennino has been applying it constantly (see papers on SMEG <http://statisticalmodelingecologygroup.blogspot.dk/p/publication.html>), and me since a while too. For further methodological/theoretical details about its application in SDMs, you may refer to Paper 1 <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00477-012-0652-3>, supplementary material of Paper 2 <http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S030438001730073X>, and/or Paper 3 <https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03787>.

I have included a detailed script in my master thesis about how to perform SDMs in INLA (unfortunately it is in Portuguese, but in case you want, I may translate it in english).
Also, feel free to contact Mrs. Pennino (or me) for further questions, or of course, the own r-inla group!

Best wishes,

Marie

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Species distribution modeling in INLA
messages.body_plain:
I'm developing a package to fit SDMs to different types of data,
including presence-only. Presence-only data is probably best modelled
as a point process ( e.g. see
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12352/abstract),
which INLA handles really well: pseudo-absences are really just points
being used in a numeric integration, and the INLA crowd showed how to
do this efficiently. The SPDE tutorial
(http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials) is a good starting point.

For the different machine learning models, as long a they can be
written as linear models, they can be fitted with INLA. There is now a
MaxNet package in R which can probably be used to get the MaxEnt
bases, if you want to poke around a bit.

Hm, I'm not sure if this is a huge help - email me if you want to know
more about my package. It's not quite ready to release into the wild,
but is close.

Bob

messages.subject: Predictions in hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
i have a situation where I want to generate predicted values from a binomial hierarchical model. I've got a model such as:

fit<- inla(y ~ x + f(group, model ="iid"), family="binomial", data=mydata, Ntrials=1)

I know from the FAQ that if I want to get fitted values from the model, I can basically include new values of 'x' in my data, with y == NA, and I will get fitted values for those cases. My question is, what about the hierarchical level? I.e. what if I have a new level of 'group' that isn't originally observed, but I want to use the posterior predictive distribution to estimate the value for a new group?

Any advice would be welcome.
-Corey

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] conditional Poisson regression model with INLA?
messages.body_plain:
>
> and I do not understand it really. is this using a multinomial
> likelihood for the conditional poisson???
>

Somehow, yes, but not quite. In my case I actually have binary data, where one success (1) is grouped with nine failures (0) to one stratum (btw, the data stem from animal movement behaviour, where at each step of a given location (1), a fixed number of possible locations (0) is added.)

Thus the response y is binary, and ten points build up a stratum. The likelihood for the analysis would be the conditional logisitic. A trick to do the analysis is to use cox regression, where all event times are set to 1. I therefore tried something like this:

formula <- inla.surv(rep(1,nn), y) ~  x1 + x2 + x3 +   strata(ID) + random terms

and used the coxph family. However, this is very inefficient, because INLA then approximates the baseline hazard by piecewise constant Poisson models, which is quite inefficient, especially because the numbers of strata is large.

Another trick is to use
formula <- y ~  x1 + x2 + x3 +   strata(ID) + random terms

and then the Poisson family, which is again giving the same results, but the problem now is that stratum-specific intercepts need to be estimated.

I'm not sure, however, if there is a way to use the Poisson family and circumvent the estimation of intercepts of each stratum... Interest does not center around them, so maybe they can be somehow fixed, but I don't see how.

messages.subject: Hypothesis testing with grouped observations
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I am trying to convince a co-author of the excellence of INLA with regard to hypothesis testing. As a starting point I have resorted to rather simple numerical cases, but these do not come out all convincing. The general question is whether I ask for the impossible, or whether there are INLA commands unknown to me which may give me what I want.

The setting is one of grouped observations. A single grouping provide the simplest possible structure for random effects and might be convincing. Data are generated with two correlated covariates, x1 with only group level values, x2 with individual values, y = x1*a1 + x2*a2 + normal noise. The true model is easily recovered with fixed-effects INLA or OLS.

The problem is to predict the value of a1 given y, x1 and grouping only, and also of a2 given y, x2 and grouping. These settings are realistic ones since few models have all the covariates observed.

When the number of groups is small relative to the number of observations, a fixed effect model (with Z as group matrix) may work,

(1)      y = x1*a1 + Z*b1 + noise1

(2)      y = x2*a2 + Z*b2 + noise2

Model (2) gives convincing values of a2 and its st.dev <http://st.dev>, while (1) does not with regard to a1. I presume these results are related to the fact that in (1) the grouping Z cannot carry complete information on the missing x2, while in (2) the grouping can carry information on the missing x1 (which is itself grouped).

Alternatively, I have tried random effects b1 and b2 with Z as effect matrix. Results are then wrong for both models. The precision of random effects becomes too high.

Questions are then: Why does (2) work while (1) does not with fixed effects? And how should the appropriate random effect models be specified?

best
Øyvind

(test file is included)

messages.subject: Re: Hypothesis testing with grouped observations
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

Let me make this post simpler. In the previous version I did ask for too much. Random or fixed effects associated with group dummies will only carry information on group level. This is why the group effect in model (1) deviates from the true model, while the individual effect in model (2) coincide.

The remaining issue is: How do I specify group effects as "fixed" and "random" so that results are equivalent?

My "fixed" effect specification is ok for relative small numbers of groups. When group numbers are counted in hundreds or thousands, the formulas will be overly long and a "random" effect is required. In low dimensions I presume equivalent specifications exist, but I have not found them. Part of the story may be related to equivalent priors. I find INLA rather vague on this, and the celebrated PC priors are not the answer in my case.

best
Øyvind

messages.subject: Interesting observation with misaligned model
messages.body_plain:
To briefly recap, I've been working on a joint binomial-binomial model for misaligned data. My primary (y) data consists of 19,000 dichotomous observations. My explanatory x variable consists of 2300 dichotomous observations. The y dataset is highly heterogeneous, with a marked cluster. The x dataset has the exact same pattern of heterogeneity and in real life may be causal. Both the y and x observations are point referenced coordinates.

Now the main difference is that y is a rare disease, the average prevalence is around 0.03 and the range when I predict a simple model is 0.02 to 0.05 over the spatial study area. X on the other hand is common, with a prevalence of about 0.5.

When I ran the simple (just y) versus the misaligned model (x  + y), the joint model is predicting a mean of around 0.5. What I would expect (or what I want to see) is that adjusting for x flattens the heterogeneity of y, so in other words the mean of y remains around 0.03 but due to the adjustment there is much less spatial heterogeneity.

> inla.zmarginal(prob.y)  ### Simple

Mean            0.028731

Stdev           0.0034379

Quantile  0.025 0.0213073

Quantile  0.25  0.0265691

Quantile  0.5   0.0289577

Quantile  0.75  0.0310783

Quantile  0.975 0.0349434

> inla.zmarginal(prob.yx)  ### Misaligned

Mean            0.509118

Stdev           0.0417084

Quantile  0.025 0.419248

Quantile  0.25  0.481496

Quantile  0.5   0.513336

Quantile  0.75  0.539668

Quantile  0.975 0.579484

So I tried an experiment. For the predictor points x, I used rbinom to generate random 1s and 0s in the same proportion as x, but obviously randomized with respect to coordinates. In other words I was more or less keeping the same dataset but killing any spatial autocorrelation of 1 or 0. I then reran the misaligned binomial-binomial model:

> inla.zmarginal(prob.rand) ### Misaligned with random x values

Mean            0.61701

Stdev           0.0150328

Quantile  0.025 0.586401

Quantile  0.25  0.607368

Quantile  0.5   0.617091

Quantile  0.75  0.626687

Quantile  0.975 0.646697

So it looks very similar to the non-randomized data, the real data.

My conclusion here is that the posterior of the combined model is heavily influenced by the proportion of 1s and 0s. It does not seem influenced by the spatial heterogeneity seen in the x dataset.

So here are my questions:
1 - Is this a reasonable interpretation? That the difference in proportions between y and x is dominating the model output to the exclusion of the spatial pattern?
2 - How do I answer my REAL question, my research question - does the spatial pattern of x explain the observed variability in y?

Thanks,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
I'm not absolutely sure that I understand your question, so let me know if the answer makes sense or not.

If you have a factor variable: "group number", you can either
1) Use fixed effects (one for each factor level, where the reference level is covered by the intercept)
2) Random effect: IID replicate over the groups (determining deviation from intercept level)

When you use the fixed effects, the priors are essentially flat. This means that if you have one group without observations, you will get an almost flat posterior (sd=31) for that fixed effect.

When you use random effect, you have a pooling parameter sigma (precision^-0.5), telling you the size of the priors. If you have a group with no observations, the posterior from this will be the prior, of the size that you determined (by sigma) through fitting the other groups.

Having the pooling parameter (1 extra hyperparameter) is generally thought to be a good idea, and the reason to use hierarchical models.

Håvards reply shows you how to make the same model in two different ways, namely by fixing the value of this pooling parameter.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

Additionally, with regards to your script (it is a bit hard to read), I note that you simulate from
>> x1 = (Z %*% rnorm(n.g))[, 1]*sd.x1

This simulates one level for each group, from the same distribution N(0, sd.x1^2). One natural way to do inference on this is to use the IID random effect (with covariate being the group number), where the precision parameter is trying to figure out what the true sd.x1^-2 is.

In this case, however, you would only supply the group identities to the data, and not x1 itself (as you did)...

Haakon

messages.body_plain:
log precision is - log(1000)

"the replication of the fixed effect results are much better than with estimated precision"

Why are they better? Better at predictions? Recover the truth inside interval?

- To me, the best model is that which you believed generated the data. Hence, if you think the group effect can be completely different, you want flat prior, but if you think they should be of the same size roughly, you want to infer parameter.
- By the way, the defualt priors are not so good. we recommend inla.doc("pc.prec"). Especially for sparse data!

"in particular with low dimensional data"

Hmm, low dimensional can mean 2 different things here
- Few groups
- Few observations per group
- Both
Which one are you talking about?
- If you have few groups, the inference about sigma/precision makes little sense, as you have no replicates to determine the size of the iid model.

messages.body_plain:
"My real data are not that sparse. There are otherwise warnings against pc priors with hypothesis testing as far as I remember? And there are also warnings against default priors.  log precision = - log(1000) give me flat prior which is neither. My follow up is whether it should be fixed or not?"

This "sparse" depends on how many observations you have per group. I would guess that if you have like 100+ observations per group, you may as well go with flat priors, as you have enough strength in the data.

You could also consider doing model comparison between the two models (fixed precision and inferred precision), e.g. with CPO or another prediction measure. There is also the possibility to stop doing hypothesis testing altogether and just do (predictive) model comparisons instead.

PS: The flat prior is still a "default prior", just of a different kind; it will sometimes overestimate the size of the effects.

Kind regards,
Haakon

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to use the iid model in a slightly different way, fixing a certain (reference) group to 0.
This is equivalent to treatment contrasts in the regular lm model in R, rather than the sum-to-zero contrasts provided by the iid model.

The idea is to get a shrinked estimator for different treatment effects in comparison with a control group.

Is this possible?

Best,
Andreas

just define the iid model for group 2...m.  for group 1 just set the
idx to NA.

like here, instead of g=1:m, use g=c(NA, 2:m), and then

f(g, model="iid")

it is not advisable however, since the implied prior is not

g=1:m
f(g, model="iid", constr=TRUE)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Joint disease mapping
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Sorry I forgot to reply to all...

> I have a problem to get the INLA syntax for modeling joint disease. There is an article
> Spatial Models with the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation within Markov Chain Monte Carlo Virgilio G´omez-Rubioa, ∗ , Francisco Palm´ı-Perales a

That paper is an application to spatial models of this more general paper:

https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.07844

> However I have a problem how to run joint disease mapping in INLA using share component approach.

The code to fit that models for a fixed set of parameters (m.delta) is below. We are using a model with 3 likelihoods for this. However, the model requires MCMC on the spatial weights, and unless you have a large dataset the model will run faster with jags or WinBUGS.

Right now I cannot give you a reproducible example because our data is confidential, but if you can find a publicly available dataset with three or more diseases (observed, expected and boundaries of areas) I'll be happy to share this.

If you have two diseases you can use the besag2 latent model to fit a similar model, I think.

Best,

Virgilio

---

fit.inla <- function(data, m.delta) {
  data$delta <- m.delta[data$r]
  form.joint <- OBS ~ -1 + rf +
    f(AREAID, model = "besag", graph = W, replicate = r,
      hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(0.01, 0.01)))) +
    f(AREAID.com, delta, model = "besag", graph = W,
      hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(0.01, 0.01))))

  res <- inla(form.joint, data = data, family = rep("poisson", 3), E = data$EXP)

  #???We need to change mlik to account for m.delta
  #res$mlik <- res$mlik - 47*sum(log(m.delta))

  return(list(mlik = res$mlik[1,1], model = res))

}

Hello,
    Thanks for your prior response. Back with a related issue. Using the same sample code:

n = 100; u <- (rnorm(n)>0) + 0; y <- rgamma(n,10); y[u==0] <- NA; dat <- list(Y=matrix(NA,2*n,2))
dat$Y[1:n,1] <- u
dat$Y[n+1:n,2] <- y
dat$mu.u <- rep(1:0, each=n)
dat$mu.y <- rep(0:1, each=n)
violation = (rnorm(n)>0) + 0

dat$u_violation <- c(violation,rep(NA,n)); dat$y_violation <- c(rep(NA,n),violation)
dat$u_revenue <- c(runif(n,0,100), rep(0,n)); dat$y_revenue <- c(rep(0,n),dat$u_revenue[1:n])

r = inla(Y ~ 0 + mu.u + mu.y + u_revenue*u_violation + y_revenue*y_violation, c('binomial', 'gamma'),data = dat, control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))

lc = inla.make.lincombs(u_violation= r$model.matrix[1:n, "u_violation"],  "u_revenue:u_violation" = r$model.matrix[1:n, "u_revenue:u_violation"])

rr = inla(Y ~  0 + mu.u + mu.y +  u_revenue*u_violation + y_revenue*y_violation,c('binomial', 'gamma'), data = dat , control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE), lincomb = lc)

I now wish to compute a posterior density for `violation + violation:revenue`, where violation is a dummy variable (basic idea is the effect of a violation on the response variable varies by revenue level). In any case, the code above produces a crash at the first linear combination where both violation and violation*revenue are 0 (i.e., the first non-violator, which makes sense since the marginal effect is then zero as well).

*** ERROR ***	Lincomb error for section[lincomb.lc001]
*** ERROR ***	All weights are zero.
	GMRFLib version 3.0-0-snapshot, has recived error no [9]
	Reason    : Invalid value of parameter
	Message   : Condition `0 == 1' is not TRUE
	Function  : inla_parse_lincomb
	File      : src/inla.c
	Line      : 8948
	RCSId     : hgid: 7e45fc2b7a2f  date: Tue Jan 31 09:14:12 2017 +0300
Aborted
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.

My question then is this: What is the appropriate procedure in this case? Is it appropriate to simply compute linear combinations only for violators (as in the code below), or does that raise other problems?

lc_violators = inla.make.lincombs(
  u_violation= r$model.matrix[which(violation==1), "u_violation"],
  "u_revenue:u_violation" = r$model.matrix[which(violation==1), "u_revenue:u_violation"])

rr = inla(Y ~  0 + mu.u + mu.y +  u_revenue*u_violation + y_revenue*y_violation,c('binomial', 'gamma'),
          data = dat ,
          control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
          lincomb = lc_violators)

Best,
-tyler

messages.body_plain:
you can add a weight, like this

f(time, weight, model="rw2")

this would give

	``weight(time) * f(time)''

so the 'regression coefficient' is the model defined in f().

H
